# Clinical Vignette: Aroha

Aroha is a thirty-year-old Māori woman who works as a licensed plumber for a commercial contracting firm. She has been married for four years to a man she describes as steady and kind — qualities she says she spent a long time not believing she deserved.

Growing up in a small town on the North Island, Aroha was raised primarily by her maternal uncle after her mother left the family when Aroha was five. By her own account, her uncle was unpredictable — generous on some days, and on others, prone to sudden, explosive violence. She describes being struck with open hands, belts, and on at least two occasions, a length of electrical cord. The abuse was rarely preceded by any clear warning. She learned early to read the atmosphere of a room the moment she walked into it, cataloguing small cues — the set of a jaw, the particular silence before a storm. She did not tell anyone. She assumed, as children often do, that this was simply what home was.

By the time she left at seventeen to complete a trade apprenticeship in Auckland, she had built what she calls a "hard shell." She was good at her work — methodical, physically capable, unbothered by tight spaces or difficult conditions. The plumbing trade suited her. She liked that problems had solutions you could see and fix with your hands.

For several years, she managed. She worked long hours, avoided close relationships, and drank more than she now thinks was healthy. The past felt distant, something left behind in another place.

The difficulties returned with force about eighteen months ago, after an incident at a job site where a supervisor — a large man with a short temper — threw a clipboard across a room during an argument with another worker. The sound, the sudden movement, the quality of the man's anger, landed somewhere deep inside her. That evening she could not stop shaking. She slept poorly for weeks afterward and began dreading going to work, scanning the site each morning before she would allow herself to fully enter.

Since then, she finds herself easily startled by raised voices, by the bang of a pipe, by any sudden movement in her peripheral vision. She describes a persistent low-level vigilance that exhausts her — an inability to sit with her back to a door, a habit of mentally mapping exits. At home, she sometimes snaps at her husband over small things and then feels flooded with shame. She worries she is becoming her uncle.

There are nights when she wakes at two or three in the morning with her heart hammering, certain something is wrong, though she cannot always say what she has dreamed. Other times the memories come to her while she is working — her hands busy threading pipe, her mind suddenly back in that house, the particular smell of it, the way she used to make herself very small and very quiet. She has learned to push through these moments, but they leave her feeling hollowed out for the rest of the day.

She does not talk about any of this easily. She describes herself as a private person and says that in her community, and in the trades especially, you do not show weakness. She came to therapy, she explains, because her husband asked her to, and because she is tired — tired of being on guard all the time, tired of the distance she feels from people she loves, tired of carrying something that happened to a child and not knowing how to put it down.

What comes through most clearly when she speaks is not fragility but a kind of worn endurance — a woman who has been strong in the only ways she knew how to be, and who is beginning to wonder, carefully and with some fear, whether there might be another way to live.
